{"differential_diagnosis": [{"diagnosis": "Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo", "confidence": 0.95}, {"diagnosis": "Posterior semicircular canalolithiasis", "confidence": 0.92}, {"diagnosis": "Anterior semicircular canalolithiasis", "confidence": 0.78}, {"diagnosis": "Horizontal semicircular canalolithiasis", "confidence": 0.75}, {"diagnosis": "Vestibular migraine", "confidence": 0.65}], "diagnostic_uncertainty": 0.142, "reasoning": "The hallmark symptom—brief, recurrent vertigo triggered specifically by changes in head position relative to gravity (e.g., rolling over in bed, looking up)—is pathognomonic for benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV). BPPV is almost always due to canalolithiasis (free-floating otoconial debris) in a semicircular canal; the posterior canal is involved in >80% of cases, making posterior canalolithiasis the most specific and likely etiologic diagnosis. Anterior and horizontal canal variants are less common but well-documented causes of positional vertigo with distinct nystagmus patterns. Vestibular migraine is included as a plausible alternative because it can present with positional vertigo (though typically less strictly tied to position change and often accompanied by other migraine features); however, its lower confidence reflects the absence of reported headache, photophobia, or aura in the provided history. Other causes like vestibular neuritis, stroke, or Meniere disease are excluded from the top 5 because they lack the strict positional trigger, involve longer-lasting symptoms, or include additional features (e.g., hearing loss, persistent imbalance) not mentioned."}

Cervicogenic dizziness is plausible given neck-position coupling but lacks supporting neck pain or restriction history. Orthostatic hypotension can cause positional dizziness but typically occurs on standing (not supine-to-lateral roll) and would more commonly involve lightheadedness than true vertigo; absence of syncope, fatigue, or antihypertensive use lowers likelihood. Superior canal dehiscence is rare and usually associated with sound- or pressure-induced vertigo (Tullio phenomenon), autophony, or hearing changes—none reported—making it the least likely."}

Posterior canal BPPV is the most common subtype (≈80–90% of BPPV cases) and fits the described triggers perfectly; horizontal canal BPPV is the second most common and may present with similar positional triggers but often with more prominent horizontal-torsional nystagmus and dizziness during rolling. Vestibular migraine is less likely given the strict positional dependence and absence of migraine features (no headache, photophobia, phonophobia, or visual aura), though it remains a diagnosis of exclusion. Orthostatic hypotension is unlikely because dizziness is not tied to upright posture change *per se* (e.g., standing from seated) but rather to specific head movements in supine/sitting positions—and the patient denies presyncope symptoms like lightheadedness, fatigue, or syncope. Central causes (e.g., posterior fossa stroke, MS) are highly improbable without neurological deficits, progressive course, or non-positional features."}
